CaseNumber: 01111943
Reported software version: Voalte Nurse Call 4.0.405
case_summary.summary: At Holy Cross Health, a code blue call in 3 South, CVIMC, Room 360 did not annunciate at the primary location. Investigation found the GRS10 serving the PBX station was repeatedly going into recovery mode, and after shared-RCB wiring was investigated and the GRS10 at the PBX was eventually replaced, the customer confirmed functionality; a Chronos report confirmed the code blue call did alert for the room, though the PBX did not see the call because the device was in recovery mode at the time.
case_summary.reported_issue: Code blue call did not annunciate at the primary staff console for the room.
case_summary.product: GRS10 / PBX station, Nurse Call system
case_summary.actions_taken: Checked that the call device, dome light, and staff console operated normally during testing.
Found no system alert present at the GRS10 during the time of the incident.
Identified that the RCB for the PBX station was shared with another location, which may have caused rebooting.
Monitored the PBX station, which did not time out during observation; ping and interface checks showed no obvious faults.
Replaced the GRS10 at the PBX, pushed software, and updated configuration in ECT.
Customer tested and confirmed functionality.
case_summary.resolution: Replacing the GRS10 resolved the issue; a Chronos report confirmed the code blue call did alert for this room.
case_summary.status: resolved
case_summary.key_points: Root cause: GRS10 at the PBX repeatedly going into recovery mode.
RA_Test_Results__c states the GRS10 at the PBX continued to go into recovery mode, which conflicts with the case resolution stating replacement resolved the issue; the case resolution and actions-to-resolve fields were preferred here.
RA_Did_same_issue_occur__c: No.
HRCSVC_Injury_or_Death__c was asked but not provided, flagging it as a safety-relevant case.

root_cause_summary: The investigation determined that Room 360 successfully generated the Code Blue call locally, and the room's relay outputs activated as expected, confirming the initiating device functioned properly. However, the call was not annunciated at the expected consoles because the communication path between the room, primary console, and PBX infrastructure was disrupted at the time of the event.

Logs showed that shortly before the incident, the 3 South primary console experienced heartbeat and handshake failures to its rooted-device communication path. At the same time, GatewayService recorded socket communication errors involving the PBX GRS10 (10.244.57.65), indicating loss of connectivity within the alert distribution path.

Further analysis of the PBX GRS10 syslog identified a known software defect related to oversized message handling. GatewayService transmitted oversized packets that triggered packet framing/deserialization failures on the PBX GRS10, causing application faults and watchdog-triggered reboots. This behavior is consistent with known defect https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/browse/NC-20964#icft=NC-20964. The resulting PBX GRS10 failure placed the device into recovery mode and prevented it from receiving or processing Code Blue events during the incident window

root_cause_summary: (1) Initial incident, 9/24/2019: two GRS5s were stuck in recovery mode. Their RCB3s generated alerts in rapid succession and sent them through the RCB3 NUC (10.190.12.156) to the GRS10 primary console (10.190.13.253), pushing CPU on the NUC and GRS10 to about 98%, causing console reboots and 15-40 second audio delays to rooms. Replacing the two GRS5s stabilized the site. (2) Recurrences on 9/28, 10/3 and 10/8 (roughly every 5 days): the NUC logged TCP write failures and deserialization errors on corrupt or partial packets, then lost RCBs, the lost primary console and repeated reboots of the 3CX PBX (10.4.204.128), until the NUC was rebooted. Engineering attributed this to the customer network (customer-owned switches with known power problems; DHCP lease behavior suspected), but it wasn't confirmed.
investigation_details: Amilcar Ubiera and Steve Moore found the two recovery-mode GRS5s flooding alerts. Disabling those rooms and replacing the GRS5s ended the spike, and the bad units were shipped back (FedEx 113944138643 / 113944138654). For the recurrences, Steve Martin captured NUC logs; Steve Moore found socket write failures and packet deserialization errors on the NUC, which points to a network problem. Open questions to the customer were never answered: confirm the NUC and 3CX server MAC addresses differ, DHCP lease renewal frequency and server type, DHCP logs matching the event times, and antivirus exclusions.
rca_review_comments: Initial cause: failed GRS5 audio stations in recovery mode caused an alert storm; corrected by replacing them. Recurrences: probable customer network or infrastructure problem, not confirmed because the customer's information was never received. Workaround: reboot the RCB3 NUC. Follow-up items: find out why the returned GRS5s couldn't leave recovery mode, and why an RCB3 sends alerts in rapid succession when its audio station malfunctions; neither has a recorded result or defect.

root_cause_summary: Root cause is blown diode D2_PWR which is a known issue for this SRS model/revision. This issue has been resolved in subsequent models and revisions (reference CRCO# C134673).
investigation_details: **HW Investigation**

Device arrived dead. Would not power up because +5V rail was shorted to Ground. Root cause is a blown diode D2_PWR, which is the catch diode for the 5V buck converter. For the P2594NNC1B11 with PCB BOM Agile PN: 164760 Rev 2, the D2_PWR component is a 60V part (MPN: LT1766EFE#TRPBF, Mfr: Linear Technology). Rev 3 of the PCB BOM contains the replacement parts which are rated at 100V – so the issue with this component was fixed by 2015/2016 model year and subsequent models (reference CRCO# C134673).

I found one similar case with this same version of the SRS (P2594NNC1B11):

* SN: 481309JWIS, NCMR0396716, Case: 23988 -- received/tested 14 June 2022
* Troubleshooting notes: “SRS is dead, no +5V. Catch diode, D2_PWR, short.  Known issue with this diode which has been corrected with alternate diode.”

Also worth noting is that the nurse station did receive a Lost Primary Audio Station Alert for ED1 and it was showing on the console prior to the Code Blue, see case in Salesforce. Therefore, the device was not functioning properly prior to the Code Blue event. Furthermore, the customer said they thought they had a pending ticket on their end to replace the device.

The site also had another SRS the month before that they asked for a replacement, serial number indicated it was the same week/year as the device for this case (04414089WIS). They rebooted the associated RCB device and the lost primary audio station alert was still present. Services team reached out multiple times to see if the replacement that was sent was installed and configured successfully for ED4 but received no response from the customer so that case (01040763) was eventually closed.

I replaced the D2_PWR with a working component and the device now passes FCT. Note that logs say partial fail because the VPD read/write test was skipped and the handset off hook test initially failed because I did not remove the handset from the FCT cradle in time and had to re-run the test – which passed on the second attempt.

Issue- PBX console (Secondary GRS10) was showing 30 lost unit server alerts. Unable to receive Code blue alerts. Checking performance of the GRS10 it remains at a constant 98/99% for CPU usage for NNC. 

Cause- The CPU usage is due to the GRS10 failing to make connections to other NNC devices over port 50005. Most of the connections show a TIME_WAIT instead of ESTABLISHED. Further probing revealed these connection failures was due to a disabled GRS10H NUC on the same subnet as our effected GRS10. 

Resolution: Rebooting the disabled GRS10H NUC resolved the issue of the failed connections on our effected GRS10. After the reboot connections were established and NNC CPU utilization on the GRS10 went down. 

Reason for RCA- We need to confirm why a disabled NUC would cause this sort of issue.
comment_summary: A basement PBX console reported Lost Unit Server alerts, together with high NNC CPU utilization on a GRS10 even though the bed plugins were not in use. Removing all plugins except calls and repeatedly rebooting the GRS10H NUC cut the alerts from 30 to 17 and finally cleared them, although the plugin-related spiking was supposed to have been resolved after 3.9.401. Later work found Lost Unit Server and lost secondary console alerts persisting for a nursing unit that was disabled in ECT, and the alerts cleared only after removing that disabled unit from the secondary unit monitoring of the other primary console and of the PBX. In the final session, re-enabling monitoring and rebooting the PBX no longer reproduced the alerts, and the engineer disabled SNTP on a POE switch (firmware 1.0.23) that had been rebooted, then left the site monitoring for recurrence.

case_summary.summary: At Scotland Memorial Hospital, a code call in 2nd Floor Med Surg Room 202 was not alerting the primary station, with no alerts or errors seen on initial console review. comment_summary: GRS5 devices connected to RS2 (port 2) of RCB3 units were not receiving configuration, while GRS5s on RS1 worked correctly; only 4 of 13 changed rooms failed, new RCBs from different batches did not help, and substituting RCB1s cleared the problem immediately. Diagnostics included a Wireshark capture during a failed software download to the port 2 GRS5 (download failed with connection lost), plus hillrom-version, ip addr and nncdiag device-configuration list output from the RCB3. The thread concludes that the device firmware version in use has a bug, fixed in Nurse Call 4.0, in the script that starts the PPP daemon for port two of an RCB3: it configures the PPP connection with up to three DNS servers when the RCB3's DHCP lease supplies three, but PPP only allows two, so the child GRS5 on port 2 gets no DNS resolution. Because DNS is used to resolve the Nurse Call server IP for device registration, the port 2 GRS5 cannot obtain configuration or software updates.

title: Lost Primary or Secondary Audio Station
text: ## Problem

---

Used when there is a Lost Primary Audio Station or Lost Secondary Audio Station system alert on the primary console and in the Enterprise Configuration Tool's (ECT) 'Active Calls' section.

- Environment: Nurse Call - All versions
- This KB may require an RCB reboot

## Solution

---

1. Determine the audio station type, serial number and RCB port number by performing the following steps:
    1. On the GRS10 console navigate to Menu → System Alerts.
    2. Highlight the **Lost Audio Station** alert and click the **Show Details** button.
    3. At the bottom of the screen note if the Audio station is a GRS5 *(gas)* or SRS *(sas)*, its serial number and RCB Port number.

         For example:*** iob-0xxxxxxxWIS:gas-0xxxxxxxWIS:1*** - where ***iob-*** is RCB serial, ***gas-*** is GRS5 serial and ***:1*** or ***:2*** represent RCB ports that the audio station is connected to - RS1 or RS2 respectively.  
  
    4. If SRS, skip to **step 6**.  
    5. If GRS5 proceed to the next step.  
  
2. Determine if GRS5 is powered on or off, online or offline by performing the following steps:
    1. [Access the command line interface (CLI) of the parent RCB device](https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/CTS/pages/888144057/How+to+connect+to+a+base+device+command+line+interface+CLI) (parent of the lost GRS5).
    2. Once at *iob *command prompt, use *ping* command. If GRS5 is in port 1 use *10.0.0.2* IP address, if in port 2 use *10.0.0.6.*
    3. If ping was unsuccessful, skip to **step 5.**
    4. If ping was successful, the GRS5 is powered on and online; proceed to the next step.  
  
3. Determine if the GRS5 is properly configured and on the correct software version by performing the following steps:
    1. [Access the CLI of the GRS5](https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/CTS/pages/907903288/How+to+Access+GRS5+GRS7+Command+Line+Interface+CLI).
    2. Once at the  `gas-xxxxxwis $`command prompt, determine if the serial number in the prompt matches the serial number from **step 1.b**.
        1. If serial numbers are mismatched, make the necessary corrections in ECT.
        2. If they are the same, proceed to the next step.
    3. In the command prompt of the GRS, type ***nnc -v*** and hit enter. Note the application software version of the GRS5.
    4. Open Service Portal or SAMM Tool and determine if GRS5 is on the correct software version with the rest of the devices.
        1. If the software is mismatched, download and apply the correct version to the GRS5.
        2. If the software matches proceed to the next step.  
  
4. [Reboot the GRS5 and the parent RCB](https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/CTS/pages/1030848709/How+To+Reboot+a+Base+Device) and wait up to 5 min for the alerts to clear.
    1. If the system alert has cleared, complete the CRM resolution fields using the tables below. If issue persists, engage a senior member of your team for further guidance before escalating.  
    2. If the system alert persists, **replace the GRS5**.  
  
5. If ping was unsuccessful, perform the following steps to determine if the GRS5 is powered off or offline.
    1. Power down the parent RCB and test cabling between RCB and GRS5 and visually inspect both ports for damage.
    2. If cable tests passed and no port damage is seen, temporarily swap RS1 and RS2 ports on the RCB and power on the RCB to determine if power is being delivered to GRS5 on the other port.
        1. If power is being delivered to GRS5 and both RS ports are being used, the RCB has a faulty RS port and it needs to be replaced.
        2. If RS2 port was open, configure the GRS5 for port 2 in ECT and publish configuration.
        3. If GRS5 still does not power on, **replace the GRS5**.  
  
6. SRS’s are not IP addressable so no ping command can be performed from its parent RCB to verify the connectivity. A simple way to confirm connectivity of an SRS is to try a PSoC software download to the SRS in Service Portal or SAMM Tool.
    1. If PSoC download is unsuccessful, skip to **step 8**.
    2. If PSoC download is successful the SRS is powered on and online. Proceed to the next step.  
  
7. In Service Portal or SAMM Tool, determine if SRS is on the correct PSoC software version.
    1. If the software matches, try rebooting the SRS via Room Reset on GRS10 or by [rebooting its parent RCB](https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/CTS/pages/1030848709/How+To+Reboot+a+Base+Device).
    2. If none of the above fixes the issue, **replace the SRS**.  
  
8. If PSoC download was unsuccessful, perform the following steps to determine if the the SRS is powered off or offline.
9. If confirmed, complete the CRM resolution fields using the table below. If issue persists, engage a senior member of your team for further guidance before escalating.

## Cause

---

Misconfigured device  
Mismatched software versions  
Faulty cabling  
Faulty RCB RS port  
Faulty device

root_cause_summary: Root cause is blown diode D2_PWR which is a known issue for this SRS model/revision. This issue has been resolved in subsequent models and revisions (reference CRCO# C134673).
investigation_details: **HW Investigation**

Device arrived dead. Would not power up because +5V rail was shorted to Ground. Root cause is a blown diode D2_PWR, which is the catch diode for the 5V buck converter. For the P2594NNC1B11 with PCB BOM Agile PN: 164760 Rev 2, the D2_PWR component is a 60V part (MPN: LT1766EFE#TRPBF, Mfr: Linear Technology). Rev 3 of the PCB BOM contains the replacement parts which are rated at 100V – so the issue with this component was fixed by 2015/2016 model year and subsequent models (reference CRCO# C134673).

I found one similar case with this same version of the SRS (P2594NNC1B11):

* SN: 481309JWIS, NCMR0396716, Case: 23988 -- received/tested 14 June 2022
* Troubleshooting notes: “SRS is dead, no +5V. Catch diode, D2_PWR, short.  Known issue with this diode which has been corrected with alternate diode.”

Also worth noting is that the nurse station did receive a Lost Primary Audio Station Alert for ED1 and it was showing on the console prior to the Code Blue, see case in Salesforce. Therefore, the device was not functioning properly prior to the Code Blue event. Furthermore, the customer said they thought they had a pending ticket on their end to replace the device.

The site also had another SRS the month before that they asked for a replacement, serial number indicated it was the same week/year as the device for this case (04414089WIS). They rebooted the associated RCB device and the lost primary audio station alert was still present. Services team reached out multiple times to see if the replacement that was sent was installed and configured successfully for ED4 but received no response from the customer so that case (01040763) was eventually closed.

I replaced the D2_PWR with a working component and the device now passes FCT. Note that logs say partial fail because the VPD read/write test was skipped and the handset off hook test initially failed because I did not remove the handset from the FCT cradle in time and had to re-run the test – which passed on the second attempt.

text: ## Problem

The screen on a GRS5/GRS7 or GRS10/10H is frozen or not responding correctly to user input.

Only when a spare device is available, proceed to the next step.

Ensure that the end user is available to help before proceeding. Proceeding with this step will result in a temporary lost device system alert, preventing it from booting up fully until the screen is calibrated.

1. Follow the steps on the linked page for [removal of the device pointercal file using WinSCP](https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/CTS/pages/917602986/How+to+remove+the+pointercal+file+via+WinSCP).

During testing, the bed-exit alarms were delayed and took longer than expected to clear, and continuous ping testing showed repeated timeouts. The system logs also show similar communication failures affecting multiple unrelated devices connected to the same service host. This points more toward an intermittent network or service-host communication problem than a confirmed RCB hardware failure.

Replacing the RCB2 units with RCB3 units restored normal operation, but the replacement also included software installation, device serialization, ECT configuration, VOIP setup, and clearing the lost-device alerts. Because several changes were made at the same time, the replacement alone does not prove that the original RCBs were defective. 

Both returned RCBs also passed Bed Exit alarm testing on the bench. Based on the available evidence, the most likely cause was an intermittent field communication or service-host issue. A permanent hardware failure in either RCB has not been demonstrated.
investigation_details: **Software Investigation:**
* Bench tested on of the returned RCB (31130NAWIS) with a GRS5 and a GRS10H and manually triggered a bed exit alarm, it rang correctly on the GRS10H and the GRS5.
* **On-site (as mentioned on Salesforce), TS found continuous ping timeouts to both RCBs** during the original screen-share investigation, with alarms "slow to alarm and slow to clear." Since the units test clean on bench, root cause is more likely related to **site network conditions** (switch/VLAN/PoE/latency) than to the RCB hardware itself.
* No ping timeouts were observed on the RCB during the bench testing.
* _Note: the site fix involved full de-registration/re-registration (remove old RCB, add new RCB to NUC, re-serialize) in addition to a physical swap. Given bench testing shows the returned RCBs function correctly, it's possible the fix resulted from re-registration/network reseat rather than a hardware defect in the RCB itself. Bed exit GRS10 ringing was never explicitly retested onsite postfix, only 2-way audio was confirmed._

This has not yet been verified against the site's ECT config and should be compared directly.~~
* ~~Testing of the second RCB unit is still pending.~~

* Syslogs were fetched from the server:

* From the syslogs it is evident that there was a network issue which caused the RCBs to go down, which caused its child devices to also not respond to the network.
verification_summary: Based on the available evidence, no hardware failure was identified in the returned RCBs. comment_summary: A site reported GRS10s emitting a three-tone beeping noise with no active calls or alerts, together with sporadic stuck calls where a call placed in one room remained active on a GRS5 in another room with no matching active call in the database. Raising APLMOD logging to level 7 on an affected RCB confirmed a tone being played repeatedly with no reference to a current call, and the stuck call cleared after rebooting the room; purging the configuration of a GRS10 resolved a beeping instance. The pattern identified was that affected calls were all configured "display at patient station: always", only old hardware was involved (GRS5 not GRS7, RCB not RCB3, AGAS not GRS10H), and it occurred in units where an AGAS acts as the NUC, suggesting a timing issue. Replacing the AGAS NUC with an RCB3 NUC in an affected unit stopped recurrences there and the approach was extended to other units, while merely turning logging up also appeared to change the timing and stop the problem; the thread concludes it is a timing issue with no single identifiable cause, expected to be corrected by the significant changes in 4.2.200.

And, while we can’t point at anyting and say “this is the cause”, things have changed significantly in 4.2.200 which is expected to correct the issue. https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/browse/NC-386#icft=NC-386 is the item the work was done under.  

[https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/browse/NC-386](https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/browse/NC-386)
investigation_details: have been looking thru logs and looking at devices where this has happened.   
  
characteristics:

1. call is placed, annunciates normally and is eventually canceled.  Call remains active on a GRS5
2. the common characteristics for call configuration so far is that they have all been “display at patient station: always”
3. only has been observed on old hardware: grs5, not grs7, rcb, not rcb3, agas not grs10h
4. happens in units that have an AGAS as a nuc
5. seems to be some sort of timing issue, this could also be a coincidence, turning up logging on devices for a unit where this happens as frequently as anywhere, which is still very infrequently, and it has not happened in that unit since.

Hospital has been adding an rcb3 nuc to units where this has happened and we have not seen a re-occurrence in those units since.
troubleshooting_steps: Received call from Sam Gormont around 8:45 am. Called Sam back. He confirmed the issue has returned with GRS10 beeping with no calls/alerts.  
Requested he confirm what console he is at. He gave the ip address 172.16.26.1 which belongs to the GRS10 NUC for 3 North.  
Further probing revealed the beeping was related to a accurate bed offline alert. Walked Sam through steps for checking call.  
Cleared alert after adjusting power cable for bed. Confirmed now we have no beeping.  
Confirmed beeping with no active calls or alerts has not reoccured since purging config consoles.  
Sam then brought up another stuck call on a GRS5. GRS5 for room W 362 is showing a call from room N 376.  
This call has been on the waitlist for 52 hours. Vnc into both GRS5s. Confirmed N 376 does not show a active call.  
Restarted messaging service on the off chance nursefollower issue could have applied. No change. Restarted Device service. No change.  
While the device service was down the GRS5 for W 362 never rebooted any alerts. It also still held on to the stuck normal call.  
Resetting audio did nothing. Placed another normal call from N 376 to W 362. Our existing normal call is the only call that shows.  
Although audio does still open between the two as of we accepted a call that we never receive. Sam did confirm he can hear the feedback on the audio station confirming audio is open.  
When checking the syslogs for evidence of audio being opened between the two devices. Did not find a voip transaction for the call.  
Sam confirmed rebooting the effected room will fix it but it will return. Requested we reboot to clear and try to replicate.  
Rebooted room W 362. Confirmed now call is cleared. Placed another normal call from N 376. No call ever appeared although audio does open still without being accepted.  
Sam confirmed this has only been a issue since upgrading. He stated prior to the upgrade they rarely had a open Nursecall case. Now they have frequent cases surrounding stuck calls.  
Confirmed i would continue to investigate but this will likely need a RCA. Sam confirmed. Checked software version for all devices. Confirmed they are all on the correct version.  
Site does have multiple lost secondary alerts. Thought this was related to a down CCD/PBX. Did not find a CCD/PBX for the site. Further probing revealed the site has multiple unserialized devices connected.
troubleshooting_results: Call is cleared but customer would like confirmation on why they are getting stuck.

Diagnostic steps were supplied to run fs_cli.exe -p voalte against the FreeSWITCH service on the Nurse Call Enterprise server to see whether RTC was routing the audio setup request to Nurse Call at all, with SIP-level tracing as the next step if it was. Because audio paths within Nurse Call, within Linq, and between them all worked, and because rebooting the audio station resolved it by forcing a re-download of staff wireless configuration, the theory settled on the audio station holding incorrect dialing information for that staff member, as happens when a staff member is assigned a Linq badge while CSA configuration in ECT is incorrect, since wireless device configuration updates do not trigger a staff mobile device assignment update. The site reported no known Wireless Device changes in ECT near the event, Gateway logs were not set to Verbose so data was limited, the issue was never reproducible, and no further occurrences were reported after an upgrade.

description: Creating RCA per request of Shannon Santana

Performing ERM migration.  Requirement is to backup warehouse, master and all datastore DB’s from old ERM SQL server and then restore to new ERM SQL server.  After restore, required to run Post-restore database utility.  During processing for datastore, Symmetric key error is encountered.



**Environment:**  Windows 2019,  VNC 4.0.404, ERM 4.7



**Solution:**  escalate to R&D to created manually create encryption key in original datastore DB.  After manual key is created, backup and restore datastore db, then proceed with post-restore utility.

Encryption key is created in initial setup of datastore.  In some instances key is not created.  No error is produced when this happens and ERM functions as expected.  The key does not effect functionality of ERM, only effects the ability to restore the datastore.
root_cause_summary: The datastore database on the existing server does not have the database master key, the encryption certificate, or the symmetric key required for column level encryption.
investigation_details: * ERM migrations require datastore databases to be backed up, restored, and then processed using the post-restore database utility. [\[RCA-1260 | Word\]](https://myfiles.baxter.com/personal/matt_tague_baxter_com/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7B91485DE7-BCA5-4153-9705-2C26D8C14A83%7D&file=RCA-1260.doc&action=default&mobileredirect=true)
* The datastore database on the existing server lacked the Database Master Key, encryption certificate, and symmetric key used for column-level encryption. [\[RCA-1260 | Word\]](https://myfiles.baxter.com/personal/matt_tague_baxter_com/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7B91485DE7-BCA5-4153-9705-2C26D8C14A83%7D&file=RCA-1260.doc&action=default&mobileredirect=true)
* During post-restore processing, the utility expected these encryption objects to exist and failed when they could not be found. [\[RCA-1260 | Word\]](https://myfiles.baxter.com/personal/matt_tague_baxter_com/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7B91485DE7-BCA5-4153-9705-2C26D8C14A83%7D&file=RCA-1260.doc&action=default&mobileredirect=true)
* Investigation determined that the encryption key should normally be created during the initial datastore setup, but in certain installations the key creation process did not occur and no error was generated at the time. [\[RCA-1260 | Word\]](https://myfiles.baxter.com/personal/matt_tague_baxter_com/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7B91485DE7-BCA5-4153-9705-2C26D8C14A83%7D&file=RCA-1260.doc&action=default&mobileredirect=true)
* Because the missing keys do not affect normal ERM operations, the issue remained hidden until a datastore restore or migration was attempted.

description: * The customer has a wireless integration from Nurse Call to Connexall via Longleaf Relay
* The customer was upgraded from NNC 3.9.200 to Voalte NC 4.0.300 on 11/16/2021

The customer alleges, and Sean Delaney the Director of Technical Services for Hillrom has confirmed, that prior to the upgrade, and going back several years, when a caregiver receives a normal priority Nurse Call alert on their wireless phone, they could choose to callback from the alert to a room device, and the alert cancels in Nurse Call.

Since the upgrade was completed callback from the wireless device no longer cancel the alert in Nurse Call.

 

The customer wants this functionality restored.  

I did want to add that I was curious if this was related to RCA-651 / Glue
root_cause_summary: The ability to cancel calls in previous versions was never intended, and is a patient safety risk, so that ability was removed.
investigation_details: Cancelling calls via wireless was an accidental bug, it was never an intended feature.   Due to patient safety reasons, that functionality was removed.
verification_summary: The cancellation of calls by wireless devices was a defect accidentally released to the field.  The code has been changed to move the calls to the reminder list instead of cancelling them.   Remote cancellation of calls by wireless devices is a patient safety risk.  
The accidentally released defect was fixed via https://hill-rom.atlassian.net/browse/GLUE-4228#icft=GLUE-4228.
